title: ephemeral inode surge & scheduler queue long-tail notes
content:
Summary:

On 2025-11-05 we observed a sustained scheduler backlog (pods Pending > normal baseline) localized to a subset of worker pools in us-east-1. Investigation showed node-level ephemeral inode exhaustion on ~6 nodes in the storage-heavy autoscaling group (gpu-work-ephemeral-2), leading to kubelet pod start stalls and long-tail scheduling latency for best-effort/guaranteed pods. Evictions were intermittent and application-visible failures were limited, but customer-facing pipelines experienced increased latency and sporadic job failures.

Why this is unusual:
- We typically monitor disk space (df -h) but not inode usage tightly.
- The pattern was not classic disk-full; nodes had free bytes but no inodes, causing overlayfs/containerd to fail creating new file entries.
- A CRON-based housekeeping job in one service was writing lots of tiny files into emptyDir mounts (log sharding), which amplified under higher traffic and created the runaway inode consumption.

Timeline (high level):
- 2025-11-05 03:12 UTC: Pager alert from scheduler-pending-count > 95th percentile for 5m.
- 03:15 UTC: On-call triage (Ruth) sees Pending pods concentrated on nodes with high pod churn.
- 03:22 UTC: kubectl describe nodes x, y, z -> "InodesAvailable: 0" on several nodes.
- 03:30 UTC: cordon/drain of two worst nodes started to reduce scheduling pressure.
- 03:45 UTC: Temporary autoscaler paused for affected pool to avoid provisioning more nodes into same ASG until remediation completed.
- 04:10 UTC: Pod-level investigation shows multiple short-lived sidecars creating many small files in /tmp and emptyDir.
- 05:00 UTC: Mitigation: restart kubelet on two nodes after cleaning orphan container data; roll-forward eviction threshold change and add inode alert.
- 07:00 UTC: Backlog returned to baseline, monitoring shows remediation holding.

Key signals and commands used during triage:
- kubectl get pods --all-namespaces --field-selector=status.phase=Pending -o wide   # find nodes/pod patterns
- kubectl describe node <node>   # check Allocatable, Capacity, Conditions, Non-terminated Pods, etc.
- ssh to node -> df -i /var/lib/kubelet /var/lib/containerd /var/lib/docker    # inode counts
- sudo find /var/lib/containerd -xdev -printf '%h\n' | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head  # find directories with many inodes
- sudo ls -niR /var/lib/containerd | head  # sampling inode numbers
- journalctl -u kubelet -o short-iso --since "2025-11-05 02:00" | grep -i inode
- kube-scheduler logs: increased "pod not admitted" / "scheduling queue length" logs.

Root cause hypothesis:
- A recently-deployed housekeeping/aggregation sidecar (service: telemetry-shard) creates per-request tiny footprint files into an emptyDir to buffer events. Under a traffic surge pattern and a minor release change that increased shard multiplicity, the sidecar created an order of magnitude more files per minute than anticipated. Combined with overlayfs metadata behavior and current GC cadence in containerd, the nodes ran out of inodes while reported disk bytes remained normal. No existing monitor caught inode pressure early enough.

Immediate mitigations applied:
1) Cordon + drain worst-affected nodes to evacuate pods and allow instance replacement.
2) Temporarily scale down telemetry-shard replicas in the affected namespace (Graceful shutdown) to stop ongoing file creation.
3) Clean up orphaned containerd overlay directories on drained nodes:
   - systemctl stop kubelet containerd
   - remove stale overlay directories under /var/lib/containerd/io.containerd.snapshotter.v1.overlayfs/snapshots/* where safe
   - systemctl start containerd kubelet
4) Restart kubelet on nodes where overlayfs returned ENOSPC for inodes after cleanup.
5) Pause autoscaler for the specific ASG while we stabilized to avoid adding more nodes with same state.

Why restart kubelet/containerd matters:
- Kubelet/containerd retain file descriptors and caches that can delay inode reclamation visibility. Restart after cleanup ensures the runtime sees reclaimed metadata.

Data collected for postmortem:
- Node inode/byte stats (df -i, df -h) for affected nodes (saved to S3: s3://redwood-sre-logs/inode-2025-11-05/)
- Containerd overlay snapshot listings (top contributors)
- Pod manifests for telemetry-shard across replicas and recent image/tags
- Recent deploy events (kubectl rollout history, GitHub PR 472 referenced)
- Kubelet and scheduler logs (+ kube-scheduler metrics: queue length, pod admit latencies)

Short-term follow-ups (next 48h):
- Add an inode usage alert: trigger when InodesAvailable < 5% for a node for 3m (prometheus node exporter metrics: node_filesystem_files_free / node_filesystem_files_total).
- Patch autoscaler to avoid scaling identical replacement instances into unhealthy pool without verification (health-check on image boot).
- Add a temporary admission webhook limit for emptyDir-backed pod file counts? (hard to enforce) instead: add PodSecurityPolicy / SCC guidelines for sidecars that write many files (document quota).
- Coordinate with telemetry team to rollback the last shard multiplicity change and add rate-limiting to file writes; provide a hasty patch to coalesce small writes into fewer files or periodically rotate to a persistent volume with higher inode capacity.

Longer-term action items:
- Evaluate inode headroom in AMI build process: baseline ephemeral root volumes with inode capacity tests.
- Add overlayfs/containerd-specific pruning as part of node shutdown/termination lifecycle to avoid accumulation.
- Recommend a new SRE runbook section: "Node inode exhaustion" with clear triage steps and commands (see draft below).
- Create a test in chaos lab that simulates high inode churn to validate monitoring and autoscaler behavior.

Draft runbook snippet: (to fold into SRE runbook repo)
1) Detect
   - Alert: node_filesystem_files_free / node_filesystem_files_total < 0.05 for >3m OR kubectl get pods Pending > baseline with nodes showing NoSchedule conditions.
2) Triage
   - kubectl describe node <node>
   - ssh to node -> df -i /var/lib/* ; check overlayfs areas (/var/lib/containerd, /var/lib/docker)
   - list top directories: sudo find /var/lib/containerd -xdev -printf '%h\n' | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head
3) Mitigate
   - cordon node
   - scale down noisy pods (if identified) in a controlled way
   - restart container runtime after cleanup if necessary
   - if many nodes affected: pause cluster autoscaler for pool
4) Recovery validation
   - watch node_filesystem_files_free metric increase
   - ensure kubelet logs show normal pod start/gc behavior and kube-scheduler queue drains
5) Postmortem
   - collect artifacts listed above, create ticket (SRE-1284) and link to deploys/PRs

Open questions / unknowns:
- Why did containerd not GC these tiny files earlier? Is GC cadence misconfigured or ineffective for this workload pattern?
- Are there kernel-level overlayfs inode behaviors that make metadata slower to reclaim under churn? (Need kernel/FS SME input)
- Should we change base AMI to use ext4 options with higher default inode density or mount /var/lib/containerd with a separate ext4 volume sized for metadata?

Notes to self / quick todo before turning this into a full postmortem:
- Pull telemetry-shard logs for the prior 48h to quantify file creation rate per pod.
- Confirm whether any other services have similar heavy small file patterns (batch jobs -> temp files).
- Draft monitoring playbook for inode rate-of-change (delta of files_free).
- Schedule a follow-up sync with telemetry team and infra/AMI owners (cc Omar, Priya).

Appendix: quick commands and example outputs captured during triage (redacted):
- df -i /var/lib/containerd
  Filesystem       Inodes  IUsed    IFree IUse% Mounted on
  /dev/nvme1n1     13107200 13107199 1    100% /var/lib/containerd

- sudo find /var/lib/containerd -xdev -printf '%h\n' | sort | uniq -c | head
  124512 /var/lib/containerd/io.containerd.snapshotter.v1.overlayfs/snapshots/1
  84231  /var/lib/containerd/io.containerd.snapshotter.v1.overlayfs/snapshots/2

- kube-scheduler logs: "scheduling queue length exceeded threshold - 490 pending pods"

If you hit this in production during oncall: prioritize cordon/drain + scale down noisy writers; collect artifacts and escalate to infra/AMI owners for follow-up.

End of notes.
